**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better?**

**To:** Engineering leadership
**From:** Infrastructure team
**Re:** Recommendation on AI compute capacity for the next two quarters

**Summary**

We recommend that we spend the next eight weeks improving utilisation of our existing hardware before committing to any new purchases. If utilisation work stalls or product demand accelerates faster than our current forecast, we should revisit procurement with a specific, evidence-backed case rather than a general sense that "we're running out."

**Where we stand**

Our cluster currently averages roughly 35% utilisation, with peaks above 80% during shared evaluation runs and long stretches near-idle overnight and on weekends. At the same time, individual teams occasionally queue for hours to get access, which creates the impression of scarcity even when the fleet as a whole is underused. Both facts are true simultaneously, and that tension is the heart of this decision. Buying more hardware would make the queuing problem disappear immediately, but it would do so at a price that locks us in for three to five years, while the underlying scheduling problem would remain unsolved and would simply scale up with the fleet.

**Cost**

The capital case for new hardware is straightforward but unforgiving. At current prices, a meaningful expansion would consume most of our infrastructure budget for the year, and depreciation begins the day the machines arrive. GPU generations turn over quickly; hardware bought today to relieve a temporary bottleneck may be worth a fraction of its cost by the time our workload stabilises. Improving utilisation, by contrast, costs engineering time we would largely spend anyway, plus some modest investment in better queueing, batching, and checkpointing tooling. Every percentage point of utilisation we recover is effectively free capacity — capacity we already paid for and are currently letting sit idle.

**Latency and reliability**

The counterargument deserves honest treatment. Utilisation improvements are not free in terms of latency. Denser packing means longer queues for interactive work, and aggressive preemption or checkpointing can add overhead to long training jobs. If our researchers lose hours to preemptions or unpredictable slowdowns, we will have traded a capital cost for a productivity cost that is harder to see but just as real. Reliability is a related concern: running hardware harder, with more job churn and more preemption, increases our exposure to failures and makes capacity planning more fragile. New hardware, by contrast, delivers immediate, predictable relief and gives us headroom for the unplanned work — a urgent customer fine-tune, a incident-driven retraining run — that always seems to arrive at the worst moment.

**Opportunity cost and reversibility**

This is where the balance tips for me. The opportunity cost of buying hardware is not just the money; it is the engineering headcount and budget we cannot spend on the product itself, and the organisational habit we would reinforce of reaching for procurement whenever scheduling gets painful. Utilisation work, by contrast, is largely reversible and incremental. If a batching change makes interactive latency worse, we roll it back. If a scheduling policy underperforms, we adjust it. None of these decisions commits us to years of depreciation. Buying hardware is the opposite: it is a large, mostly irreversible bet that our current demand curve is durable, at a moment when our workload mix is still shifting quarter to quarter.

**What we should actually do**

Concretely: instrument the fleet properly so we can distinguish genuine scarcity from scheduling friction; introduce a shared queue with sensible priority classes so interactive work is not starved by batch jobs; and target 60% sustained utilisation as our threshold for revisiting procurement. That target is somewhat arbitrary, but it gives us a concrete, measurable trigger rather than a feeling. We should also price out a short-term cloud rental option as a pressure valve — renting for a spike is expensive per hour but trivially reversible, which makes it a better fit for uncertainty we cannot yet quantify.

**Uncertainty**

I want to be clear about what I do not know. Our demand forecast has been wrong in both directions before, and if a new product line lands in the next quarter, utilisation work will look like fiddling while capacity burns. The honest position is that we are choosing which uncertainty to live with: the financial and strategic risk of an irreversible purchase, or the operational risk of a busier, more contended fleet. On balance, the second risk is cheaper to carry and easier to shed. Let's spend eight weeks proving that, and keep the purchase decision on the table with better data behind it.

**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better?**

**To:** Engineering Leadership
**From:** Infrastructure Team
**Re:** Recommendation on AI compute capacity for the next two quarters

**Status and problem**

Our four A100 nodes are running at roughly 55% average utilisation, but that number hides the real problem. During peak hours — typically late morning when the fine-tuning queue collides with the inference fleet serving internal tools — we saturate. Researchers wait hours for jobs to schedule, and at least twice last month a batch inference job degraded latency enough that the internal search assistant felt broken to its users. Meanwhile, overnight and weekend utilisation drops below 20%. The instinctive response is to buy two more nodes. That instinct deserves scrutiny before we spend roughly $180,000.

**The case for buying**

The strongest argument for new hardware is reliability. Our current fleet has no meaningful headroom, so any hardware failure — and we had one node down for six days in March waiting on a replacement fan assembly — immediately turns into a capacity crisis. A second argument is opportunity cost of people's time. If our twelve researchers collectively lose even an hour a day to queueing, that's a real cost, and at loaded salary rates it's not obviously smaller than the amortised cost of new hardware. Buying is also simple: it requires no behavioural change, no new tooling, and no difficult conversations about who gets priority.

**The case for better utilisation**

But the utilisation data suggests we can capture much of that benefit without spending. Three things stand out. First, our scheduling is naive: jobs are assigned whole nodes even when they need a fraction of one, and we have no mechanism to preempt low-priority work. MIG partitioning and a proper priority queue are weeks of work, not months, and would likely lift effective utilisation by 20–30 points. Second, our batch workloads are not latency-sensitive and could run exclusively in the overnight trough, which we currently leave mostly idle. Third, we have never measured whether our inference fleet is sized correctly; it may be over-provisioned relative to actual traffic.

The cost side of this path is modest — perhaps three to four engineer-weeks, which is real but recoverable. The latency risk to interactive services can be managed by hard-partitioning capacity so batch work can never starve inference. And critically, this path is reversible. If we invest in scheduling and measurement and still find ourselves saturated, we will know precisely why, and the case for buying hardware will be grounded in evidence rather than anecdote. Hardware, by contrast, is largely irreversible: it depreciates, consumes power and rack space, and commits us to a maintenance relationship with a specific vendor for years.

**Uncertainty**

I want to be honest about what we don't know. Our utilisation numbers come from coarse sampling and may understate contention. Demand is also growing — two teams have signalled they want training runs this quarter that would each occupy a node for several days. If that demand materialises, better scheduling buys us time but not a solution. There is also a risk that the engineering effort to improve utilisation proves harder than estimated; scheduler work has a way of expanding. Finally, hardware prices and availability are volatile, and waiting six months could mean paying more — though the recent trend has been in our favour.

**Recommendation**

Spend the next six weeks on utilisation: implement MIG partitioning, a priority-aware scheduler, and a policy that moves batch workloads into off-peak windows. Instrument everything so we can measure the result. In parallel, draft but do not execute a purchase order for two nodes, so that if the data shows genuine saturation after the improvements land, we can move quickly with leadership's prior context rather than starting the conversation from zero.

This sequencing costs us little, preserves the option to buy, and replaces a $180,000 decision made under frustration with one made under measurement. If the researchers' queueing pain persists after the improvements, we will buy — and we'll do it knowing exactly what we're buying and why. I'd like a decision by end of week so we can start scheduler work immediately.

Happy to walk through the utilisation data with anyone who wants the detail.

I want to lay out our thinking in full, because the answer is less obvious than either the "just buy GPUs" or "just schedule better" camps assume, and because the decision is more reversible in one direction than the other.

Start with cost. Our current fleet of eight accelerators was purchased at roughly the peak of pricing, and we carry them on the books with depreciation, power, and cooling running to a meaningful monthly figure. Measured honestly, our average utilisation sits near thirty percent, with sharp peaks around model refreshes and long troughs overnight and on weekends. Buying more hardware at current prices would roughly double our fixed costs before we see a single additional job complete. Improving utilisation, by contrast, costs engineering time — scheduler work, better queueing, batch consolidation, and some unglamorous profiling — which is expensive in attention but cheap in cash. On pure cost grounds, the second option wins decisively, and it wins more the longer hardware prices continue their downward drift. There is a real chance that in twelve months the accelerator we'd buy today is available for meaningfully less, which makes deferral itself a kind of saving.

Latency is the strongest argument on the other side, and we should take it seriously. Our interactive workloads — the internal copilot, ad-hoc fine-tuning experiments, the evaluation harness engineers run before merging — suffer when queues build. Waiting forty minutes for a job that should take four is a genuine productivity tax, and it falls on our most expensive people. But when we dug into the queue data, most of the latency pain came from contention at predictable times, not from absolute scarcity. Jobs were stacking up because two teams launched long batch runs simultaneously, not because the fleet was genuinely saturated. That is a scheduling problem wearing a capacity costume. If, after we fix scheduling, p95 wait times remain unacceptable, that residual is the honest signal to buy against — and we'll have a much better estimate of how much to buy.

Reliability cuts both ways. More machines mean more redundancy: a single failed node today takes out a third of our training capacity, and our mean time to repair is measured in days because we have no spare. That fragility is real and I don't want to minimise it. But utilisation improvements help here too — checkpointing discipline, automatic job migration, and a small warm-spare pool carved out of reclaimed idle time would blunt most single-failure scenarios without new capital. The reliability case for buying is strongest if we buy one additional node specifically as a hot spare, which is a far cheaper intervention than doubling the fleet.

The opportunity cost of the engineering time is the honest counterweight. The two engineers best placed to do the scheduler work are also the people our model team wants for the upcoming release. Spending their next six weeks on infrastructure plumbing is a real trade. My view is that it's still the right trade, because the scheduler work compounds — every future team and every future workload benefits — whereas hardware purchased to paper over poor scheduling locks in the inefficiency.

Finally, reversibility. Buying hardware is close to irreversible at our scale: resale values for used accelerators are poor, and the depreciation clock doesn't stop because our needs changed. Scheduler and utilisation work is fully reversible — if it fails, we've lost time, not capital, and we can still buy later with better information. If the measurement work in the first two weeks contradicts our assumptions, we should stop and reconsider rather than press on. The point of this path is not that buying is wrong; it's that we should buy only when we can say precisely what we're buying and why.

Latency is the strongest argument on the buy side, and I want to take it seriously.
